level1.text: The threshold voltage of an orange LED is $1.95\,\text{V}$. The elementary charge is $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. How much energy does an electron receive from the voltage source when it passes across this voltage? Give the answer in joules.

The peak of the spectrum of a green LED is at the wavelength $525\,\text{nm}$. Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. How great is the energy of a photon of this wavelength? Give the answer in electronvolts.
The wavelength of the light of a red laser diode is $650\,\text{nm}$. The speed of light is $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$. What is the frequency of the light? Give the answer in hertz.

The energy gap of gallium arsenide is $1.42\,\text{eV}$. An LED made of it emits photons whose energy is approximately equal to the energy gap. Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$. What is the wavelength of the light of the LED? Give the answer in nanometres.

A student fitted to the threshold voltages of LEDs as a function of frequency a line whose slope is $k = 4.10 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s}$. The elementary charge is $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. What value did the student get for the Planck constant? Give the answer in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$.

A red LED is connected to a gradually increasing voltage. Below $1.5\,\text{V}$ the LED does not glow at all, but after about $1.8\,\text{V}$ it lights up. What explains why the LED lights up only at the threshold voltage?
level1.answer: A photon can be produced only when the energy $eU$ received by the electron is approximately equal to the energy $hf$ of the photon.

choices.text: Light is produced by heating: the LED starts to glow only when the voltage $U$ has heated the semiconductor hot enough.
choices.feedback: Heating is not the reason. The light of an LED is not the light of a glowing hot object; it is produced when an electron drops from the conduction band into a hole in the valence band and gives up its energy as a photon. A photon can be produced only when the energy $eU$ of the electron is sufficient.

choices.text: Photons are produced already at a small voltage $U$, but they are infrared, and as the voltage increases their frequency rises to red.
choices.feedback: This is a common misconception. The energy of a photon is determined by the energy gap of the semiconductor, not by the voltage, so the colour of the light of the same LED does not change when the voltage is adjusted. Increasing the voltage above the threshold increases the current and thus the number of photons.

choices.text: A photon can be produced only when the energy $eU$ received by the electron is approximately equal to the energy $hf$ of the photon.
choices.feedback: Correct: the energy of one photon is approximately $hf$, and it comes from one electron. If the energy $eU$ is smaller, no photon is produced. At the threshold voltage $eU_\text{k} \approx hf$, and after that the current and the amount of light increase steeply.

choices.text: Photons are produced already at a small voltage $U$, but the casing of the LED absorbs them until the current is large enough.
choices.feedback: The casing does not absorb light in this way. Below the threshold voltage the electrons do not receive enough energy, so no photons are produced at all. The threshold voltage is the condition for producing a photon, not a property of the casing.

level1.text:
The threshold voltage of a green LED is $2.30\,\text{V}$. Assume that at the threshold voltage the energy that an electron receives from the voltage source is exactly the energy of one photon, $eU_\text{k} = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$.

Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

What is the wavelength of the light of the LED? Give the answer in nanometres.

A current of $10.0\,\text{mA}$ flows through an LED used as an indicator light. The elementary charge is $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. How many electrons pass through the LED in a second? Give the answer in the form $x \cdot 10^{16}\,\tfrac{1}{\text{s}}$ and write the number $x$ in the box.

level2.text: The peak of the spectrum of a blue LED is at the wavelength $470\,\text{nm}$. Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. Estimate how great a voltage must at least be connected to the LED for it to start to emit light. Give the answer in volts.

The peak wavelength of an orange LED is $605\,\text{nm}$, and its threshold voltage is measured to be $1.95\,\text{V}$. Use the values $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$. What value for the Planck constant is obtained from this one LED, when $eU_\text{k} = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ is assumed? Give the answer in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$.

A current of $20\,\text{mA}$ flows through a red LED, and the wavelength of its light is $630\,\text{nm}$. Assume that every electron passing through the LED creates one photon that gets out of the LED.

Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

How great is the light power of the LED? Give the answer in milliwatts.

A white LED contains a blue LED whose photons have the wavelength $450\,\text{nm}$. It is covered by a phosphor that absorbs a blue photon and emits by fluorescence a yellow photon whose wavelength is $560\,\text{nm}$.

Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$.

How much energy per photon is left in the phosphor as heat? Give the answer in electronvolts.

The current–voltage characteristic of a red LED was measured by connecting the LED in series with a protective resistor and gradually increasing the voltage. The table is sample data. In the graph $(U, I)$ the current is at first almost zero and then increases almost linearly.

Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

a) Draw the graph $I(U)$ on paper and decide which points belong to the linear part.

b) Fit a line to the linear part and extend it to the voltage axis, where $I = 0$. Read the threshold voltage $U_\text{k}$.

c) The peak wavelength of the LED is $650\,\text{nm}$. Calculate the voltage $\tfrac{hc}{e\lambda}$ and compare it with the measured threshold voltage.

Write in the box the threshold voltage of part b) in volts.

data.caption: Current of a red LED as a function of voltage (sample data)

level2.text:
A group measured the current–voltage characteristic of a red LED whose peak wavelength is $630\,\text{nm}$.

Three students read the threshold voltage from it in different ways (table, sample data). Aino read as the threshold voltage the voltage at which the current is $0.1\,\text{mA}$, Eero fitted a line to the straight part of the graph and extended it to the voltage axis, and Salla read the voltage at which the current is $10\,\text{mA}$.

Assume $eU_\text{k} = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$. Use the values $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$ and the accepted value of the Planck constant, $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$.

a) From the threshold voltage of each student, calculate the Planck constant $h = \tfrac{eU_\text{k}\lambda}{c}$.

b) Which of the reading methods are incorrect and why? Explain why Aino’s reading is too small and Salla’s too large.

c) Calculate by what percentage the Planck constant given by Salla differs from the accepted value.

Write in the box the deviation of part c) as a percentage.

data.caption: Threshold voltage with different reading methods (sample data)

level2.text:
The spectrum of a red LED was measured with a spectrometer. The table gives the relative intensity $I_\text{rel}$ at different wavelengths, with the greatest intensity set to the value $1.00$ (sample data).

Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

a) Draw the spectrum on paper and read the wavelength $\lambda_\text{p}$ of the peak. Why is the wavelength of an LED given as the wavelength of the peak and not as a colour estimated by eye?

b) Read the width of the spectrum as the difference between the wavelengths at the two points where the intensity is half of the maximum. Compare the result with the width of the spectrum of a laser diode, about $1\,\text{nm}$.

c) Calculate the difference $\Delta E$ between the energies of the photons at these two points and use it to explain why an LED is not monochromatic.

Write in the box the energy difference of part c) in electronvolts.

data.caption: Spectrum of a red LED (sample data)

level3.text:
A group measured the threshold voltages of four LEDs.

Red LED: $\lambda = 625\,\text{nm}$, $U_\text{k} = 1.86\,\text{V}$. Yellow: $590\,\text{nm}$ and $1.97\,\text{V}$. Green: $520\,\text{nm}$ and $2.27\,\text{V}$. Blue: $465\,\text{nm}$ and $2.55\,\text{V}$.

Use the values $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

Determine the Planck constant by fitting a line to the points $(f, U_\text{k})$, for example with Graphical Analysis Pro. Give the answer in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$.

A student estimates the uncertainty of the Planck constant by drawing, for the points $(f, U_\text{k})$, the steepest and the gentlest line that still pass through the uncertainty bars of the points.

The slope of the steepest line is $4.25 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s}$ and that of the gentlest $3.95 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s}$. The elementary charge is $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

How great is the uncertainty $\Delta h$ of the Planck constant, when it is estimated as half the difference of the values given by these lines? Give the answer in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$.

An ultraviolet LED with the wavelength $365\,\text{nm}$ is used to check fluorescent markings. A current of $20\,\text{mA}$ flows through the LED, and it emits ultraviolet radiation with the power $15\,\text{mW}$.

Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

What percentage of the electrons passing through the LED create a photon that gets out of the LED?

A group measured the threshold voltages of five LEDs as the extension of the line of the current–voltage graph (table, sample data).

The zero point of the voltmeter was off: when the terminals of the meter were short-circuited, the meter showed $+0.05\,\text{V}$, so all the measured voltages are $0.05\,\text{V}$ too large.

Use the values $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$ and the accepted value of the Planck constant, $6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$.

a) Calculate the frequencies $f = \tfrac{c}{\lambda}$ and fit a line to the measured points $(f, U_\text{measured})$, for example with Graphical Analysis Pro. Record the slope and the intercept on the vertical axis.

b) Correct the voltages by subtracting the zero-point error and fit the line again. Which of the characteristics of the line changes and which does not?

c) Calculate the Planck constant from the slope of the line and its deviation from the accepted value as a percentage.

d) Also calculate the Planck constant from the threshold voltage of the red LED alone with the formula $h = \tfrac{eU_\text{k}\lambda}{c}$, before and after the correction. Using your results, justify why the Planck constant should be determined from the slope of the line and not from a single LED.

Write in the box the Planck constant obtained in part c) from the slope of the line, in the unit $\text{J}\,\text{s}$.

data.caption: Threshold voltages of LEDs with the zero-point error of the meter (sample data)

level3.text:
A measurement made with LEDs in class gave for the line between the threshold voltage and the frequency, $U_\text{k} = kf + b$, the slope $k = 4.15 \cdot 10^{-15}\,\text{V}\,\text{s}$ and the intercept $b = -0.10\,\text{V}$ (sample data).

The threshold voltage of an unknown LED was measured with the same method as $U_\text{k} = 2.46\,\text{V}$, with a measurement uncertainty of the voltage of $\pm 0.05\,\text{V}$. A spectrometer showed the peak of the spectrum of the LED at $483\,\text{nm}$.

Use the values $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $e = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$.

a) Calculate the frequency and the wavelength of the light of the unknown LED using the calibration line.

b) Also calculate the wavelength from the equation $eU_\text{k} = \tfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ and compare both with the result of the spectrometer. Which method is better and why?

c) Estimate the uncertainty of the wavelength of part a) when the voltage may be off by $0.05\,\text{V}$.

Write in the box the wavelength of part a) in nanometres.
